entries.name: Signed download link
needs: let a user download their file without making it public
the PDF link should stop working after a day
the files in my bucket are public
share a private file with one person
entries.summary: A URL with an expiry time and a signature built in. Anyone with the link can download until it expires, and changing any part of it breaks the signature. The files stay private by default.
need_when: User uploads, invoices, exports, paid downloads, anything you don't want indexed or shared forever.
skip_when: The files are meant to be public, like marketing images or open docs.

ways.title: Presigned URLs from object storage
ways.how: S3, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean Spaces and self-hosted MinIO or Garage all support S3-style presigned GET links.
ways.tradeoff: Fast and offloads bandwidth. Anyone holding the link can use it until it expires, so keep expiry short.

ways.title: Your app checks access and streams the file
ways.how: Check login and ownership, then send the file, or hand it to the proxy with X-Accel-Redirect or X-Sendfile.
ways.tradeoff: Access is checked on every download. Large files tie up app workers unless the proxy serves them.

ways.title: Sign your own links
ways.how: Django signing (TimestampSigner), Rails signed ids, or a JWT with an exp claim on a download route.
ways.tradeoff: You write the checks yourself. Rotating the key kills every outstanding link, which is sometimes what you want.

entries.prompt:
Serve [file type] privately with expiring download links.

Requirements:
- The bucket or folder is private. No public ACLs or public bucket policy.
- When a logged-in user asks for a file, check they own it, then create a presigned GET URL that expires in [15 minutes].
- Set Content-Disposition so it downloads with a safe filename.
- Keep the storage keys on the server. The frontend only ever gets the short-lived URL.
- Log who created a link for which file and when. Don't log the URL itself.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. The object's plain URL without a signature returns 403.
2. A new link works, then returns 403 after it expires.
3. Changing one character of the path or signature returns 403.
4. User A can't get a link to user B's file by changing the id.
5. Signed URLs don't show up in server logs or analytics.
acceptance_checks: The object's plain URL without a signature returns 403.
A new link works, then returns 403 after it expires.
Changing one character of the path or signature returns 403.
User A can't get a link to user B's file by changing the id.
Signed URLs don't show up in server logs or analytics.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Private files get indexed, guessed or shared forever, and you can't take a link back.

links.title: AWS: sharing objects with presigned URLs

entries.name: Direct-to-storage uploads
needs: large uploads time out on my server
let users upload videos without going through my backend
my server runs out of memory when people upload files
upload straight to S3 or R2 from the browser
entries.summary: Your server hands the browser a short-lived signed URL, and the browser sends the file straight to object storage. Your app never holds the bytes, so big files don't tie up workers or hit request size limits. Your server still decides who can upload, what key the file gets and how big it can be.
need_when: Users upload files bigger than a few MB, like photos, video or PDFs.
Your host caps request size or time, as most serverless platforms do.
skip_when: Uploads are small and rare, and your server checks the contents anyway before storing them.

ways.title: Presigned PUT URL
ways.how: S3, Cloudflare R2, Google Cloud Storage and most S3-compatible stores can sign a PUT URL for one object key that expires in minutes. The browser PUTs the file, then tells your server it's done.
ways.tradeoff: Simplest. A plain PUT URL can't enforce a size range, so check the object size after upload and delete anything too big.

ways.title: Presigned POST with a policy
ways.how: S3's POST policy can require a content-length-range and a key prefix, so the store itself rejects files that are too big.
ways.tradeoff: Enforces size up front. Not every S3-compatible store supports it. R2 presigned URLs don't support POST.

ways.title: Resumable uploads
ways.how: The tus protocol (tusd server, Uppy client) or S3 multipart uploads send the file in chunks and resume after a dropped connection.
ways.tradeoff: Best for very large files and phones on bad networks. More moving parts.

entries.prompt:
Change [feature] so files upload straight from the browser to [S3/R2/GCS] instead of through the app server.

Requirements:
- New endpoint: the logged-in user asks for an upload. The server checks they're allowed, picks the object key itself (never from the client, e.g. uploads/<user_id>/<random>), and returns a signed URL that expires in [10] minutes.
- Limit size: use a POST policy with content-length-range if the store supports it. Otherwise check the object size when the upload is confirmed and delete it if it's over [50 MB].
- After upload, the browser calls a confirm endpoint. The server checks the object exists, records it in the database with its owner, and only then shows it in the app.
- Uploaded objects stay private. Downloads go through signed download links.
- A cleanup job deletes objects that were never confirmed after [24] hours.
- Set the bucket's CORS rules to allow PUT (or POST) only from the app's own origin.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A 200 MB file uploads without the app server's memory or request time growing.
2. A file over the size limit is rejected or deleted, and never shows up in the app.
3. The signed URL stops working after it expires.
4. Changing the key in the request can't overwrite another user's file.
5. An unconfirmed upload is removed by the cleanup job.
acceptance_checks: A 200 MB file uploads without the app server's memory or request time growing.
A file over the size limit is rejected or deleted, and never shows up in the app.
The signed URL stops working after it expires.
Changing the key in the request can't overwrite another user's file.
An unconfirmed upload is removed by the cleanup job.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Uploads fail on big files, workers stall while bytes stream through them, or a bucket left open lets anyone write to it.

links.title: AWS: uploading objects with presigned URLs

entries.name: Image resizing and thumbnails
needs: my page loads 8 MB photos as tiny avatars
make thumbnails of uploaded pictures
images make my site slow on phones
photos from phones show up sideways
entries.summary: Making smaller copies of uploaded images at the sizes your pages show, in modern formats, so pages load fast. Do it once when the image arrives, or on request through an image service that caches the result.
need_when: Users upload photos and you show them in lists, cards or avatars.
skip_when: You only show a few images you made yourself. Export them at the right size once.

ways.title: Resize on upload
ways.how: A background job uses sharp (Node) or Pillow (Python) to write a few fixed sizes, like 200, 800 and 1600 px wide, as WebP or AVIF next to the original.
ways.tradeoff: Cheap to serve. Adding a new size later means reprocessing old images.

ways.title: Self-hosted image proxy
ways.how: imgproxy or thumbor resizes on request from a URL with the size in it. Put a CDN in front so each size is made once.
ways.tradeoff: Any size, any time. Sign the URLs so strangers can't make your server render huge images.

ways.title: Managed image service
ways.how: Cloudflare Images, Cloudinary, imgix, or your host's built-in optimizer (for example next/image on Vercel).
ways.tradeoff: Least work. Priced per image or per transform, which grows with traffic.

entries.prompt:
Add thumbnails and responsive images for user uploads in [feature].

Requirements:
- When an image is uploaded, a background job creates [200, 800, 1600] px wide versions in WebP, keeping the aspect ratio. Never upscale.
- Apply the EXIF orientation before resizing so phone photos aren't sideways. Strip EXIF metadata (including GPS location) from the resized copies.
- Refuse images over [40] megapixels before decoding them fully, to avoid decompression bombs.
- Store the sizes with predictable keys next to the original and record them in the database.
- In the HTML, use srcset and sizes so the browser picks the smallest file that fits, with width and height set to avoid layout shift, and loading="lazy" below the fold.
- Until the job finishes, show a placeholder, not the full original.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A 12 MB phone photo shows in a list as a file under 100 KB.
2. A photo taken in portrait shows the right way up.
3. The resized files have no GPS data (check with exiftool).
4. A 20,000 x 20,000 px image is refused without the worker running out of memory.
5. Lighthouse shows no 'properly size images' warning on the page.
acceptance_checks: A 12 MB phone photo shows in a list as a file under 100 KB.
A photo taken in portrait shows the right way up.
The resized files have no GPS data (check with exiftool).
A 20,000 x 20,000 px image is refused without the worker running out of memory.
Lighthouse shows no 'properly size images' warning on the page.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Slow pages and big bandwidth bills from full-size photos, sideways pictures, and leaked home locations in photo metadata.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: For each uploaded image, Custody Journal stores an encrypted 400 px JPEG thumbnail (quality 82) made with Pillow. It keeps the EXIF capture time and location on purpose, because those details can matter as evidence.

entries.name: Upload validation and scanning
needs: someone could upload a virus or a script as a profile picture
check that an uploaded file is really a PDF
a huge zip file crashed my server
only allow images and PDFs
entries.summary: Checking every uploaded file on the server before you keep it: its real type from its bytes, its size, and its contents where that matters. Then store it under a name you choose and serve it so the browser can't run it as a page.
need_when: Users can upload anything, and other people or your own code will open those files.
skip_when: Never fully. Even avatar uploads need a type and size check.

ways.title: Check type, size and structure in code
ways.how: Read the first bytes (python-magic, file-type for Node) and compare with an allowlist. Cap size and image pixels. Re-encode images with Pillow or sharp, which drops anything hidden in them.
ways.tradeoff: Stops most problems cheaply. Doesn't detect known malware inside a valid file.

ways.title: Antivirus scan
ways.how: ClamAV (clamd) scans each file in a background job before it's marked ready.
ways.tradeoff: Catches known malware. Needs memory and signature updates, and misses new threats.

ways.title: Storage provider scanning
ways.how: Managed malware scanning on your bucket from your cloud provider or a scanning service.
ways.tradeoff: No servers to run. Costs per GB scanned.

entries.prompt:
Harden file uploads in [feature].

Requirements:
- Allow only [PDF, JPEG, PNG, WebP]. Detect the type from the file's bytes, not the extension or the Content-Type header. Reject anything else with a clear message.
- Cap size at [25 MB]. For images, refuse anything over [40] megapixels before fully decoding it.
- For zip-based files (DOCX, XLSX), cap the number of entries and the total expanded size, and reject paths containing ../.
- Store files under a random key you generate. Never use the uploaded file name as a path.
- Serve downloads with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, from storage or a separate domain, never as HTML on the app domain.
- Optional: scan with ClamAV in a background job and keep the file hidden until it passes.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A .exe renamed to photo.jpg is rejected.
2. An HTML file uploaded as an image never renders as a page on the app domain.
3. A zip bomb is rejected quickly without filling the disk.
4. A file named ../../etc/passwd is stored under a random key.
5. If ClamAV is on, the EICAR test file is caught.
acceptance_checks: A .exe renamed to photo.jpg is rejected.
An HTML file uploaded as an image never renders as a page on the app domain.
A zip bomb is rejected quickly without filling the disk.
A file named ../../etc/passwd is stored under a random key.
If ClamAV is on, the EICAR test file is caught.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Stored cross-site scripting, malware passed on to other users, and servers knocked over by zip or image bombs.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal checks file types from the bytes, caps uploads at 50 MB and refuses images over 40 million pixels. It inspects Office files' zip contents (entry count, expanded size, compression ratio, path traversal, macros) and parses PDFs in a separate process with an 8 second timeout. It doesn't run an antivirus scanner.

entries.name: Backups with a tested restore
needs: what happens if my database gets deleted
I have backups but never tried restoring one
take a backup before I deploy
back up user uploads too
entries.summary: A backup only counts once you have restored it. Back up the database and uploaded files on a schedule, copy them off the server, and regularly restore into a throwaway database to prove they work.
need_when: You store anything users would be upset to lose.
skip_when: The data can be rebuilt from somewhere else.

ways.title: pg_dump on a schedule, shipped off the server with restic
ways.how: A nightly pg_dump and an archive of uploads, encrypted and deduplicated by restic into object storage.
ways.tradeoff: Simple. You lose whatever changed since the last dump.

ways.title: Continuous WAL archiving
ways.how: pgBackRest (or similar) for point-in-time recovery.
ways.tradeoff: More setup. Worth it when losing hours of data is not acceptable.

ways.title: Managed database backups
ways.how: A managed Postgres such as DigitalOcean's takes automated backups.
ways.tradeoff: Less to run, but you still have to test a restore, and uploaded files need their own backup. A server snapshot is not the same as a tested database restore.

entries.prompt:
Add backups with an automated restore test for [Postgres database + uploads folder].

Requirements:
- Nightly job: pg_dump in custom format plus an archive of uploaded files, taken together so they match.
- Encrypt and copy off the server to [bucket]. Keep [7 daily and 4 weekly].
- Write a manifest per run with file checksums.
- Restore test job: start a disposable Postgres, restore the latest backup into it, run a migrations check and a few row-count queries, then delete it. Record pass or fail.
- Refuse to run the restore test against anything that isn't the disposable database.
- Alert if the last good backup is older than [26 hours] or the last passing restore test is older than [8 days].
- Before each deploy, take a backup and stop the deploy if it fails.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Restoring last night's backup into a scratch database shows a row created yesterday.
2. Pointing the restore test at the production database URL makes it refuse to run.
3. Backup files can't be read without the key.
4. Turning off the backup job triggers the stale-backup alert.
5. A deploy with a failed backup stops before migrations run.
acceptance_checks: Restoring last night's backup into a scratch database shows a row created yesterday.
Pointing the restore test at the production database URL makes it refuse to run.
Backup files can't be read without the key.
Turning off the backup job triggers the stale-backup alert.
A deploy with a failed backup stops before migrations run.
entries.if_you_skip_it: You find out the backups were empty or unreadable on the day you need them.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal's release runbook makes a matched database and media backup a hard gate before any release. Its encrypted manifest has to pass a restore into a disposable PostgreSQL container, and an attest command records that result. The app's operations health report flags a failed or uncommitted latest backup. There is also a command for copying backups off the server.

entries.name: Safe database migrations
needs: change a column without breaking the live app
rename a field in production
my migration locked the table for minutes
my agent edited an old migration file
entries.summary: Changing the database schema in small steps that the old and new versions of your code can both live with, checked in CI and run as a release step. Renames and drops happen in two releases: add the new shape, move the code and data, then remove the old shape.
need_when: Your app has real data and you change models after launch.
skip_when: Before launch with throwaway data, where resetting the database is fine.

ways.title: Your framework's migrations, checked in CI
ways.how: Django migrations, Rails migrations, Alembic, Prisma Migrate or Drizzle Kit. CI fails if models changed without a migration (for example makemigrations --check) and runs all migrations on a fresh database.
ways.tradeoff: Standard and enough for most apps. The tools don't stop slow or unsafe operations by themselves.

ways.title: A linter for unsafe migrations
ways.how: strong_migrations (Rails), django-migration-linter, or Squawk for raw Postgres SQL flag table locks, non-concurrent indexes and drops of columns still in use.
ways.tradeoff: Catches the ones that cause outages. Adds a few rules to learn.

ways.title: Expand and contract by hand
ways.how: Release 1 adds the new column and writes to both. A backfill copies old rows. Release 2 reads the new column. Release 3 drops the old one.
ways.tradeoff: No downtime for renames and type changes. Takes several releases.

entries.prompt:
Set up safe migrations for this app and plan the change to [describe schema change].

Requirements:
- CI fails if a model changed without a migration, and runs every migration on an empty database.
- Never edit a migration that has already run in production. Fix forward with a new one.
- Split renames, type changes and drops into expand and contract steps that work with both the old and new code during a deploy.
- Create indexes on large tables without locking writes (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on Postgres).
- Backfill large tables in batches in a background job, not inside the migration.
- Migrations run as one release step before the new code takes traffic, and a backup is taken first.
- Write down for each migration whether it can be reversed.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. CI fails when I change a model and skip the migration.
2. All migrations apply on a fresh database with no errors.
3. During the deploy, the old code keeps working against the new schema.
4. A test copy of production data migrates in a known time without long locks.
5. The plan lists which steps are reversible.
acceptance_checks: CI fails when I change a model and skip the migration.
All migrations apply on a fresh database with no errors.
During the deploy, the old code keeps working against the new schema.
A test copy of production data migrates in a known time without long locks.
The plan lists which steps are reversible.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Deploys that take the app down, locked tables, columns dropped while old code still reads them, and migration histories that differ between machines.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal has a migration check script that fails on conflicting or missing migrations, runs every migration forward on a throwaway SQLite database, runs a full rollback and forward cycle when every step is reversible, and proves that irreversible migrations stop a rollback. Its release runbook never reverses migrations: rolling back code is allowed only after a preflight check proves the previous version runs on the new schema.

entries.name: Database connection pooling
needs: too many connections error from Postgres
my serverless functions run out of database connections
the database is slow to connect on every request
entries.summary: Reusing a small set of open database connections instead of opening a new one for each request. Postgres handles a limited number of connections, and serverless functions can open hundreds at once, so a pooler sits in between and shares a few real connections.
need_when: You run on serverless or many workers and see 'too many connections'.
Each request spends noticeable time connecting to the database.
skip_when: One long-running server with a few workers that keep their connections open.

ways.title: Persistent connections in your app
ways.how: Django CONN_MAX_AGE, or Django 5.1+'s built-in pool option with psycopg[pool], SQLAlchemy's pool, or a single shared Prisma client per process.
ways.tradeoff: Enough for normal servers. Doesn't help when every function invocation is a new process.

ways.title: Your host's pooler
ways.how: Supabase (Supavisor), Neon and most managed Postgres providers give a pooled connection string. Use it for app traffic and the direct one for migrations.
ways.tradeoff: One-line change. Transaction mode breaks session features like some prepared statements, LISTEN and advisory locks held across queries.

ways.title: PgBouncer
ways.how: Run PgBouncer next to Postgres in transaction pooling mode and point the app at it.
ways.tradeoff: Fast and proven. One more service to run and monitor.

entries.prompt:
Fix database connection limits for this app on [host].

Requirements:
- Count the maximum connections we could open: processes or functions times pool size per process. Compare with the database's max_connections and show the math.
- Use [the host's pooled connection string / PgBouncer in transaction mode] for app traffic, and a direct connection for migrations.
- Check the code for features that break under transaction pooling (session settings, LISTEN/NOTIFY, prepared statements, advisory locks) and fix or document each.
- In serverless code, create one database client per process, not per request.
- Close or reset inherited connections after a worker forks.
- Add a health check that fails if the database can't be reached.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A load test of [100] concurrent requests produces no 'too many connections' errors.
2. The connection count in pg_stat_activity stays under the planned limit during the test.
3. Migrations still run over the direct connection.
4. Nothing in the code depends on session state that the pooler would break.
acceptance_checks: A load test of [100] concurrent requests produces no 'too many connections' errors.
The connection count in pg_stat_activity stays under the planned limit during the test.
Migrations still run over the direct connection.
Nothing in the code depends on session state that the pooler would break.
entries.if_you_skip_it: The app goes down under a traffic spike with 'too many connections', or every request pays the connection setup time.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal doesn't run a separate pooler. Django keeps each connection open for up to 10 minutes (conn_max_age 600), and the Gunicorn fork hooks close database and cache connections inherited from the parent process so workers never share one.

entries.name: Soft delete and restore
needs: a user removed something by mistake and wants it back
add a trash folder with restore
undo a delete
entries.summary: Marking a record as deleted instead of removing it, so it disappears from the app but can be restored. A purge job removes it for real after a set time, which also matters when someone asks you to erase their data.
need_when: Users delete things they might want back.
Support keeps getting 'I deleted it by accident' requests.
skip_when: The data is cheap to recreate, or must be gone at once for privacy reasons.

ways.title: A deleted_at column and a default filter
ways.how: Add deleted_at, make the default query hide rows where it's set, and keep a separate way to reach all rows for admin and purge.
ways.tradeoff: Simple. Every raw query, join and unique constraint has to remember the filter.

ways.title: A library
ways.how: django-safedelete, Rails' discard gem, or Prisma query extensions.
ways.tradeoff: Less code to write. Learn how it treats related records.

ways.title: Move rows to an archive table
ways.how: On delete, copy the row to a trash table and delete the original. Restore copies it back.
ways.tradeoff: Main queries stay simple. Restoring rows with relations takes more work.

entries.prompt:
Add soft delete with restore to [model].

Requirements:
- Add deleted_at (nullable, indexed). Deleting sets it instead of removing the row.
- The default query everywhere hides deleted rows. Admin and the purge job use an explicit all-rows query.
- Unique constraints only apply to rows that aren't deleted (a partial unique index on Postgres).
- Add a Trash view where the owner can restore items within [30] days.
- A daily job permanently deletes rows that have been in the trash longer than [30] days, including their files.
- An account deletion request skips the trash and removes the data for good.
- Log who deleted and restored what.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A deleted item disappears from lists, search and the API.
2. Restoring brings it back with its related data.
3. Creating a new item with the same unique name as a deleted one works.
4. After the retention period the purge job removes it and its files.
5. Grep shows no raw queries that skip the deleted filter.
acceptance_checks: A deleted item disappears from lists, search and the API.
Restoring brings it back with its related data.
Creating a new item with the same unique name as a deleted one works.
After the retention period the purge job removes it and its files.
Grep shows no raw queries that skip the deleted filter.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Deleted items come back in search or counts, unique names stay taken forever, or 'deleted' data is still there when someone asks you to erase it.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal's journal entries, custody events and communications share a soft-delete base with is_deleted and an indexed deleted_at. The default manager hides deleted rows, and a separate all_objects manager is used for admin, migrations and purging. Admin actions restore selected items, and soft deletes are written to the audit log.

entries.name: Audit log
needs: see who changed a record and when
a customer says they didn't edit this, prove it
keep a history of admin actions
show an activity feed of changes
entries.summary: An append-only record of important actions: who did what to which record, when, and from where, with the values before and after. It answers support questions and security reviews, and some customers require it.
need_when: Several people can edit the same data, or admins can act on user accounts.
Customers ask for compliance features or you handle sensitive records.
skip_when: A single-user app with no admin tools, where ordinary logs are enough.

ways.title: An audit table you write to
ways.how: A table with actor, action, target type and id, before and after values, IP and time. Write to it in the same transaction as the change.
ways.tradeoff: Full control over what's recorded. You have to call it from every place that matters.

ways.title: A history library
ways.how: django-simple-history, PaperTrail (Rails), or Postgres triggers that copy old rows into a history table.
ways.tradeoff: Captures every model change automatically. Doesn't capture who unless you pass the user in, and stores a lot.

ways.title: An audit log service
ways.how: Hosted audit log products like WorkOS Audit Logs, often used when enterprise customers ask for exports.
ways.tradeoff: Exports and customer-facing views built in. Another vendor holding sensitive data.

entries.prompt:
Add an audit log for [models/actions].

Requirements:
- Record actor (user id or 'system'), action (create, update, delete, plus named actions like role_changed), target type and id, changed fields with before and after values, IP, user agent and UTC time.
- Write the audit row in the same transaction as the change, so neither can exist without the other.
- Never store passwords, tokens, API keys or full card data. Mask or hash sensitive fields.
- The audit table is append-only for the app: no update or delete code paths, and no edit form in admin.
- Add a page where [admins / the account owner] can filter the log by user, record and date.
- Keep entries for [1 year], then delete them with a scheduled job.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Editing a record creates one audit row with the right before and after values.
2. A failed edit that rolls back leaves no audit row.
3. No secret or token appears anywhere in the audit table.
4. The app has no route that edits or deletes audit rows.
5. The filter page finds all changes to one record.
acceptance_checks: Editing a record creates one audit row with the right before and after values.
A failed edit that rolls back leaves no audit row.
No secret or token appears anywhere in the audit table.
The app has no route that edits or deletes audit rows.
The filter page finds all changes to one record.
entries.if_you_skip_it: No way to answer 'who did this', disputes you can't settle, and failed security reviews. A log that stores secrets becomes a leak of its own.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal logs create, update and delete for six models (entries, communications, custody events, children, documents and reports) when the change comes from a signed-in request. Each row keeps the previous and current data, IP, user agent and session key. Encrypted fields are stored as an HMAC fingerprint, so the log shows that a field changed without holding the text.

entries.name: Transactions and race conditions
needs: a double click created two orders
two requests at once let a user spend more credits than they have
the free plan limit can be beaten by sending requests in parallel
half my data saved and the rest didn't
entries.summary: Making a group of database changes all happen or none happen, and making sure two requests running at the same moment can't both pass a check that only one should pass. Check-then-write code is the usual bug: both requests read the old value before either writes.
need_when: You check a balance, quota, stock count or 'already used' flag and then change it.
One action writes to more than one table.
skip_when: Single writes with no check before them, like saving a draft.

ways.title: Atomic conditional updates
ways.how: Do the check inside the write: UPDATE accounts SET credits = credits - 1 WHERE id = ? AND credits >= 1, then see whether a row changed.
ways.tradeoff: Fast, no locks held. Only fits checks that one statement can express.

ways.title: Transaction with a row lock
ways.how: Open a transaction, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the row that guards the rule (the user, the account), check, write, commit.
ways.tradeoff: Handles complex rules. Keep it short, and lock rows in the same order everywhere to avoid deadlocks.

ways.title: Unique constraints and idempotency keys
ways.how: A unique index on (user_id, request_key) or on the natural key makes the second insert fail. The client sends the same key on a retry.
ways.tradeoff: Stops duplicates even across servers. Needs a key the client keeps for the action.

entries.prompt:
Find and fix race conditions in [feature, e.g. credits, checkout, invites].

Requirements:
- List every place that reads a value, checks it, then writes based on it (balances, quotas, stock, 'used' flags, unique names).
- Fix each with a conditional update, a row lock inside a transaction, or a unique constraint. Say which and why.
- Wrap multi-table writes in one transaction.
- Give create actions an idempotency key so a double click or retry doesn't create two records.
- Disable the submit button while a request is in flight, but don't rely on it.
- Write a test that fires [20] parallel requests at each fixed action.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. 20 parallel 'spend 1 credit' requests on a balance of 5 leave exactly 0 and succeed 5 times.
2. Double clicking 'Place order' creates one order.
3. Killing the process halfway through a multi-table write leaves no partial data.
4. Parallel requests can't push a free account past its limit.
acceptance_checks: 20 parallel 'spend 1 credit' requests on a balance of 5 leave exactly 0 and succeed 5 times.
Double clicking 'Place order' creates one order.
Killing the process halfway through a multi-table write leaves no partial data.
Parallel requests can't push a free account past its limit.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Negative balances, duplicate orders and charges, free limits that a script can beat, and half-saved records.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal checks the free plan's monthly entry limit while holding a row lock on the user (select_for_update), so parallel requests can't both use the last slot. A sign-in link is marked used with a conditional update that only succeeds while it's still unused and unexpired, so it can't be used twice.

entries.name: Pagination
needs: my list page loads every row and got slow
add load more or infinite scroll
page 500 of the results is really slow
items show up twice when I scroll
entries.summary: Returning a list a page at a time instead of all at once. Offset paging (page 3 of 20) is simple and fine for small lists. Cursor paging (give me the 25 after this one) stays fast on big tables and doesn't skip or repeat items when rows are added while someone scrolls.
need_when: Any list or API that can grow past a few hundred rows.
skip_when: Lists with a hard small cap, like a user's 5 saved addresses.

ways.title: Offset and limit
ways.how: LIMIT 25 OFFSET 50, or your framework's paginator. Shows page numbers and a total.
ways.tradeoff: Easy. Deep pages get slow on big tables, and rows shift when new ones arrive.

ways.title: Cursor (keyset) pagination
ways.how: Sort by a unique, indexed key like (created_at, id) and return a cursor for the last row. The next page asks for rows after it.
ways.tradeoff: Fast at any depth and stable while data changes. No jumping to page 37.

ways.title: Search engine paging
ways.how: If the list comes from a search service, use its own paging and result limits.
ways.tradeoff: Fits search results. Totals are often estimates.

entries.prompt:
Add pagination to [list page / API endpoint].

Requirements:
- Use cursor pagination ordered by (created_at, id) descending, with an index that matches that order. The response includes items and next_cursor (null on the last page).
- Page size defaults to [25] and the client can't ask for more than [100].
- The cursor is opaque to the client (base64-encoded) and is validated on input.
- Keep the user's filters and ownership check on every page.
- In the UI, add a 'Load more' button (or infinite scroll that also has a button for keyboard users).
- If page numbers are required, use offset paging only for this small list and say why.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. The first request returns 25 items and a next_cursor.
2. Following cursors to the end returns every item exactly once, even if new items are added during the walk.
3. Asking for 10,000 items returns at most 100.
4. EXPLAIN shows the query uses the index on deep pages.
5. A tampered cursor returns 400, not a server error.
acceptance_checks: The first request returns 25 items and a next_cursor.
Following cursors to the end returns every item exactly once, even if new items are added during the walk.
Asking for 10,000 items returns at most 100.
EXPLAIN shows the query uses the index on deep pages.
A tampered cursor returns 400, not a server error.
entries.if_you_skip_it: List pages that time out as data grows, APIs that return a million rows, and feeds that repeat or skip items.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal pages its long lists with Django's Paginator, mostly 25 rows per page, which is offset paging.

links.title: Use The Index, Luke: paging through results

entries.name: Rate limiting
needs: someone keeps trying passwords on my login
a bot is hammering my AI endpoint and my bill went up
limit each user to 10 generations an hour
stop spam on my signup form
entries.summary: Count requests per key (IP address, user or API key) in a time window and refuse with 429 once the count passes the limit.
need_when: Login, signup, password reset and one-time codes.
Any endpoint that costs you money per call: LLMs, email, SMS.
Public forms.
skip_when: Static pages served from a CDN.

ways.title: Rules at the edge
ways.how: Cloudflare WAF rate limiting rules block by IP before traffic reaches your server.
ways.tradeoff: Stops floods cheaply, but only sees IPs and paths, not your logged-in users or plans.

ways.title: Counters in your app, stored in Redis
ways.how: Fixed or sliding window counters in Redis or your shared cache. Libraries: django-ratelimit, express-rate-limit with a Redis store.
ways.tradeoff: Can key on user id and plan. In-memory counters reset on restart and aren't shared between processes, so use Redis.

ways.title: Usage quotas in the database
ways.how: Count generations per user per month in a table and check it before the expensive call.
ways.tradeoff: Right for paid limits. It is billing logic, so it needs tests.

entries.prompt:
Add rate limiting to [endpoints].

Requirements:
- Use a shared store (Redis) so limits hold across processes and restarts.
- Limits: [login: 5 tries per 15 minutes per IP and per account], [AI endpoint: N per hour per user].
- Get the client IP correctly behind our proxy. Only trust X-Forwarded-For when the request comes from our proxy, and take the address our proxy added (counted from the right), not the leftmost one.
- Return 429 with a Retry-After header and a plain message.
- For login, reset and code entry, fail closed: if the counter store is down, refuse the attempt.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. The 6th login attempt inside 15 minutes returns 429.
2. Sending a made-up X-Forwarded-For header doesn't reset the limit.
3. Limits still apply after restarting the app.
4. With Redis stopped, login refuses attempts instead of allowing unlimited tries.
5. Normal use (browsing, one login) never sees a 429.
acceptance_checks: The 6th login attempt inside 15 minutes returns 429.
Sending a made-up X-Forwarded-For header doesn't reset the limit.
Limits still apply after restarting the app.
With Redis stopped, login refuses attempts instead of allowing unlimited tries.
Normal use (browsing, one login) never sees a 429.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Password guessing, scraped content, and a surprise bill when a bot finds your AI endpoint.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal uses fixed-window counters in the Redis cache it already runs, with no extra library, and hashes the counter keys. Security-sensitive limits fail closed: if the counter store is unavailable, the request is denied. The client IP comes from X-Forwarded-For only when the request arrives from a trusted proxy, counted from the right by the number of proxy hops, so a spoofed header can't dodge the limit.

entries.name: Ownership checks (IDOR)
needs: change the id in the URL and see someone else's data
make sure users can only edit their own posts
my API returns any record if you know the id
are UUIDs enough to keep records private
entries.summary: Checking on every request that the logged-in user is allowed to touch the exact record they asked for. The usual bug: the code loads a record by id and never checks who owns it. Hard-to-guess ids help but don't replace the check.
need_when: Any URL or API with a record id in it.
skip_when: The record is public on purpose.

ways.title: Put the owner in the query
ways.how: Load records with the owner in the filter, like get(id=..., owner=current_user), so another user's id finds nothing and returns 404.
ways.tradeoff: Simple and hard to get wrong once it's a habit. Every new endpoint must follow it.

ways.title: A scoped helper or manager
ways.how: One function, for_user(user), that every query starts from. Code review flags any query that doesn't use it.
ways.tradeoff: Makes the safe path the easy path. Admin and background code need a clearly named way around it.

ways.title: Database row level security
ways.how: Postgres RLS policies as a backstop, so even a buggy query can't return other users' rows.
ways.tradeoff: Strong. Needs the user identity passed into the database session.

entries.prompt:
Audit and fix object-level authorization in this app.

Requirements:
- List every route and API endpoint that takes a record id (path, query string or body).
- For each, load the record with the current user (or their tenant) in the query. Another user's id must return 404, not the record and not a 403 that confirms it exists.
- Check nested ids too, like an attachment id inside a request for a note the user owns.
- Writes and deletes get the same check as reads.
- Add a test per endpoint: user A creates a record, user B tries to read, edit and delete it.
- Produce a table of endpoints with the check used and the test name.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. User B gets 404 for user A's record on every endpoint in the table.
2. Changing an id inside a JSON body (not only the URL) is blocked.
3. File and download endpoints check ownership the same way.
4. List endpoints never include other users' rows, even with filters changed.
5. The test suite covers every endpoint in the table.
acceptance_checks: User B gets 404 for user A's record on every endpoint in the table.
Changing an id inside a JSON body (not only the URL) is blocked.
File and download endpoints check ownership the same way.
List endpoints never include other users' rows, even with filters changed.
The test suite covers every endpoint in the table.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Anyone can read or change other users' records by counting up ids. Broken object level authorization is the first item on the OWASP API Security Top 10.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal loads user records with the owner in the query, for example get_object_or_404(Entry, pk=pk, user=request.user), so another user's id returns 404.

links.title: OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

entries.name: Input validation
needs: users can send any data to my API
someone made themselves admin by adding a field to the request
validate form data on the server too
a huge request crashed my server
entries.summary: Checking every piece of incoming data on the server against what you expect: type, length, format and allowed values. Anything else is rejected before your code uses it. Browser checks only help the user. Anyone can skip them.
need_when: Every form, API endpoint, webhook and file import.
skip_when: Never on the server. Even internal endpoints get called with bad data eventually.

ways.title: A schema at each endpoint
ways.how: Zod or Valibot (TypeScript), Pydantic (Python) or JSON Schema. Parse the body into the schema and use only the parsed result.
ways.tradeoff: Clear and typed. You need the habit of never reading the raw body after parsing.

ways.title: Your framework's forms or serializers
ways.how: Django forms or DRF serializers with explicit field lists, Rails strong parameters, Laravel validation.
ways.tradeoff: Built in. 'All fields' shortcuts bring back mass assignment.

ways.title: Database constraints as the last line
ways.how: NOT NULL, CHECK constraints, foreign keys, unique indexes and column lengths.
ways.tradeoff: Catches what code misses. Errors arrive late and are less friendly.

entries.prompt:
Add server-side input validation to [endpoints/forms].

Requirements:
- Define a schema for each endpoint's input: types, required fields, max lengths, allowed values, number ranges.
- Reject unknown fields. Never copy request data straight onto a model. Set allowed fields one by one (no mass assignment of role, owner_id, is_admin or price).
- Cap request body size at [1 MB] unless the endpoint needs more.
- Use parameterized queries or the ORM everywhere. No SQL built from strings.
- Return 400 with a field-by-field message the UI can show. Don't echo raw input back into HTML.
- Add database constraints for the rules that must never break.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Sending is_admin=true or a different owner_id in the body changes nothing.
2. A 10,000-character name is rejected with a clear message.
3. A body over the size cap returns 413.
4. Searching for ' OR 1=1 -- returns a normal empty result.
5. Every endpoint in the app is listed with its schema.
acceptance_checks: Sending is_admin=true or a different owner_id in the body changes nothing.
A 10,000-character name is rejected with a clear message.
A body over the size cap returns 413.
Searching for ' OR 1=1 -- returns a normal empty result.
Every endpoint in the app is listed with its schema.
entries.if_you_skip_it: People give themselves admin rights, store junk that breaks pages, or crash the server with huge requests.

entries.name: CORS settings
needs: blocked by CORS policy error in the browser
my frontend on one domain can't call my API on another
is Access-Control-Allow-Origin star safe
entries.summary: Headers your API sends to tell browsers which other websites may read its responses. CORS only loosens the browser's same-origin rule. It doesn't stop scripts, servers or curl from calling your API, so it never replaces authentication.
need_when: Your frontend and API are on different origins (domain, subdomain or port) and the browser blocks the call.
skip_when: Frontend and API share one origin, for example the API lives at /api on the same domain. Then you need no CORS headers at all.

ways.title: Serve both from one origin
ways.how: Route /api to the backend through your host's rewrites or a reverse proxy, so the browser sees one site.
ways.tradeoff: No CORS to get wrong, and cookies just work. Needs a proxy or rewrite rule.

ways.title: Framework CORS middleware with an allowlist
ways.how: django-cors-headers, the cors package for Express, or FastAPI's CORSMiddleware, with an explicit list of allowed origins.
ways.tradeoff: Standard. Easy to loosen to * during debugging and forget.

ways.title: CORS at the edge
ways.how: Set the headers in Nginx, Caddy or a Cloudflare rule in front of the API.
ways.tradeoff: Works for any backend. Keeps rules away from the code that needs them.

entries.prompt:
Fix CORS for the API at [api origin] used by [frontend origins].

Requirements:
- Allow only these exact origins: [list], read from config per environment. No wildcard, and never reflect the request's Origin header back without checking it against the list.
- If the browser sends cookies, set Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. That requires a specific origin, never *.
- Allow only the methods and headers the frontend uses, and handle OPTIONS preflight requests.
- Add Vary: Origin when the response depends on the origin.
- Explain in a comment that CORS is not access control. Every endpoint still checks authentication.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. The real frontend can call the API with no CORS errors in the console.
2. A request with Origin: https://evil.example gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.
3. curl -X OPTIONS with an allowed origin returns the expected allow headers.
4. No response anywhere has Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with credentials.
acceptance_checks: The real frontend can call the API with no CORS errors in the console.
A request with Origin: https://evil.example gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.
curl -X OPTIONS with an allowed origin returns the expected allow headers.
No response anywhere has Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with credentials.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Either the frontend can't reach the API, or a wide-open setting lets any website read signed-in users' data through their browser.

entries.name: CSRF protection
needs: another website could submit forms on my site as the logged-in user
CSRF token missing or incorrect error
do I need CSRF protection if I use cookies for login
entries.summary: Stopping other websites from making a logged-in user's browser send state-changing requests to your app. It matters when login lives in cookies, because the browser attaches them automatically. APIs that only accept a token in the Authorization header aren't exposed in the same way.
need_when: Your app uses cookie sessions and has forms or endpoints that change data.
skip_when: The API accepts only bearer tokens in a header and never reads a cookie for auth.

ways.title: Your framework's built-in protection
ways.how: Django's CsrfViewMiddleware, Rails' protect_from_forgery, or Laravel's CSRF middleware. Next.js server actions compare the Origin and Host headers by default, but your own route handlers need their own check.
ways.tradeoff: Proven. Exemptions added to silence errors are where the holes appear.

ways.title: SameSite cookies plus Origin checks
ways.how: Set session cookies to SameSite=Lax or Strict and reject state-changing requests whose Origin header isn't yours.
ways.tradeoff: Strong defence in modern browsers. Best used together with tokens, not instead of them.

ways.title: Header-only token auth
ways.how: Keep the auth token out of cookies and send it in the Authorization header from your own code.
ways.tradeoff: Not exposed to CSRF. The token then has to be kept away from cross-site scripting.

entries.prompt:
Audit and fix CSRF protection in this app.

Requirements:
- Confirm the framework's CSRF protection is on for every route that changes data (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
- List every CSRF exemption with the reason. Keep an exemption only if the endpoint authenticates another way (a webhook signature, or a bearer token with cookies refused).
- No GET request changes data. Move any that do to POST.
- Session cookies use Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax (or Strict).
- Set the trusted origins list for production domains only.
- Add a test that posts a form without the token and expects 403.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A form posted from another origin without a token is rejected.
2. Every CSRF exemption is listed with how that endpoint authenticates instead.
3. Grep shows no GET handler that writes to the database.
4. The session cookie shows Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite in the browser's dev tools.
acceptance_checks: A form posted from another origin without a token is rejected.
Every CSRF exemption is listed with how that endpoint authenticates instead.
Grep shows no GET handler that writes to the database.
The session cookie shows Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite in the browser's dev tools.
entries.if_you_skip_it: A malicious page can change a user's email, delete data or make purchases using the user's own logged-in browser.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal keeps Django's CSRF middleware on for the whole site, and production trusted origins default to the site's own https domains. The exemptions are the Stripe webhook (checked by signature), a small anonymous analytics endpoint, OAuth endpoints for an integration, and mobile API endpoints that refuse cookie sessions and accept only bearer tokens. Sign-in links use a POST confirm step, so a GET never logs anyone in.

entries.name: Secrets management
needs: I committed my API key to GitHub
where do I put my Stripe secret key
my OpenAI key is visible in the browser
rotate a leaked key
entries.summary: Keeping API keys, passwords and signing keys out of your code, your git history and the browser. They live in your host's secret settings or a secrets manager, the app reads them at startup, and you know how to replace each one quickly if it leaks.
need_when: Your app talks to any paid API, database or payment provider. That's almost every app.
skip_when: Never.

ways.title: Host environment variables
ways.how: Set secrets in Vercel, Netlify, Render, Fly or your server's env, keep .env in .gitignore, and commit a .env.example with names only.
ways.tradeoff: Enough for most apps. Copies spread across environments and people's laptops.

ways.title: A secrets manager
ways.how: Infisical (open source), Doppler, 1Password Secrets Automation, or your cloud's secret manager inject secrets at deploy time.
ways.tradeoff: One place to rotate and audit. Another service your deploys depend on.

ways.title: Leak prevention
ways.how: Turn on GitHub secret scanning and push protection, and run gitleaks in a pre-commit hook or CI.
ways.tradeoff: Catches mistakes before they ship. Doesn't help with a key that's already public: that one must be rotated.

entries.prompt:
Clean up how this app handles secrets.

Requirements:
- Find every secret in the code, config files and git history (run gitleaks or a similar scanner). List them by name only. Never print a value.
- Move each to environment variables read at startup. Add a .env.example with the names and no values, and make sure .env is in .gitignore.
- Make sure no secret reaches the browser: check client bundles and any NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_ or similar prefixed variables. Calls that need a secret key go through the server.
- The app fails to start in production if a required secret is missing, and the error names the variable, not its value.
- For any secret found in git history, write the rotation steps (create a new key, deploy, revoke the old one). Removing it from history is not enough.
- Turn on secret scanning and push protection for the repo.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. gitleaks reports no secrets in the working tree.
2. Searching the built frontend bundle finds no secret key prefixes (like sk_live_ or sk-).
3. Starting the app without a required secret fails with a message naming it.
4. Logs and error pages never show a secret value.
acceptance_checks: gitleaks reports no secrets in the working tree.
Searching the built frontend bundle finds no secret key prefixes (like sk_live_ or sk-).
Starting the app without a required secret fails with a message naming it.
Logs and error pages never show a secret value.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Leaked keys get found and used fast: surprise AI bills, stolen data and abused payment accounts.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal refuses to start in production without a SECRET_KEY. A check script validates each service's environment before deploy, fails closed, and reports only variable names and the service role, never values. Key files must be absolute paths with mode 0400 or 0600, and backup encryption keys have IDs so older keys can still decrypt after a rotation.

entries.name: SSRF protection
needs: my app fetches a URL the user pastes in
build link previews safely
users can set their own webhook URL
import an image from a URL
entries.summary: Guarding any feature where your server fetches a URL that a user supplied. Without it, someone can point your server at internal addresses, like a cloud metadata endpoint or an admin panel on localhost, and read the response through your app.
need_when: Link previews, 'import from URL', user-set webhook URLs, PDF or screenshot rendering of user URLs, or an AI tool that browses.
skip_when: Your server only calls fixed URLs that you wrote in the code.

ways.title: Resolve, check, then connect to that IP
ways.how: Allow only https, resolve the host, reject any private, loopback, link-local or reserved address, then connect to the checked IP so a second DNS answer can't swap it. Don't follow redirects, or check each hop the same way.
ways.tradeoff: Strong. Easy to get subtly wrong, so use a tested helper and test it.

ways.title: An outbound proxy with rules
ways.how: Send user-URL fetches through a proxy like Smokescreen that blocks internal ranges, and give the app no other route out for those calls.
ways.tradeoff: One choke point for every feature. Another service to run.

ways.title: An allowlist of domains
ways.how: Only fetch from a known list, like the image hosts or integrations you support.
ways.tradeoff: Safest. Too narrow for general link previews.

entries.prompt:
Add SSRF protection to every place this app fetches a user-supplied URL ([features]).

Requirements:
- One shared fetch helper. All user-URL fetches go through it.
- Allow only https (http only in local development). Reject URLs with a username or password in them.
- Resolve the hostname with a time limit, and reject if any resolved address is private, loopback, link-local (including 169.254.169.254), multicast or reserved, for both IPv4 and IPv6.
- Connect to the IP you checked, not the hostname again, to block DNS rebinding.
- Don't follow redirects, or re-run every check on each redirect target with a limit of [3].
- Set a total timeout of [10] seconds and a response size cap of [1 MB].
- Never return raw error details or the internal response to the user.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. http://127.0.0.1, http://localhost and http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ are all rejected.
2. A hostname that resolves to 10.0.0.5 is rejected.
3. A public URL that redirects to an internal address is rejected.
4. IPv6 forms like http://[::1]/ are rejected.
5. A slow server is cut off at the timeout, and a huge response at the size cap.
acceptance_checks: http://127.0.0.1, http://localhost and http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ are all rejected.
A hostname that resolves to 10.0.0.5 is rejected.
A public URL that redirects to an internal address is rejected.
IPv6 forms like http://[::1]/ are rejected.
A slow server is cut off at the timeout, and a huge response at the size cap.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Attackers read cloud credentials from the metadata service, reach internal admin tools, or scan your private network through your app.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal's outgoing webhooks go through an SSRF guard. It requires https (http only in debug), rejects URLs with embedded credentials, resolves the host with a 5 second limit, and refuses if any resolved address isn't a public one. It then connects to the checked IP, never follows redirects, and caps each call at 10 seconds and a 64 KB response.

entries.name: Bot and spam protection
needs: bots are signing up thousands of fake accounts
my contact form gets spam
add a captcha to signup
someone is testing stolen card numbers on my checkout
entries.summary: Stopping automated traffic on forms that cost you money or reputation: signup, login, contact, checkout and anything that sends email or calls an AI. Layers work best: a hidden honeypot field, a challenge like Turnstile checked on the server, and rate limits behind both.
need_when: You see bursts of fake signups, spam messages, or failed card attempts.
A form triggers something that costs money, like an email, SMS or AI call.
skip_when: Low-traffic internal tools behind a login.

ways.title: Honeypot field and timing
ways.how: A field hidden from people that bots fill in, plus a check that the form wasn't submitted in under a second or two.
ways.tradeoff: Invisible to users. Only stops simple bots.

ways.title: Turnstile, hCaptcha or reCAPTCHA
ways.how: Add the widget, then verify the token on your server with the provider's siteverify API before doing anything. Cloudflare Turnstile tokens are single-use and expire after 300 seconds.
ways.tradeoff: Stops most automated abuse. A widget that isn't verified on the server does nothing.

ways.title: Rate limits and verification
ways.how: Limit by IP and by account, require email verification before the account can do costly things, and use your payment provider's fraud tools on checkout.
ways.tradeoff: Catches what gets past the challenge. Needs tuning so real users aren't blocked.

entries.prompt:
Add bot protection to [signup / contact / checkout] forms.

Requirements:
- Add a honeypot field hidden with CSS (not type=hidden), with tabindex=-1 and autocomplete=off so people and password managers skip it. Reject submissions that fill it, with a generic message.
- Add Cloudflare Turnstile (or hCaptcha). On the server, verify every token with the siteverify endpoint before any other work. Reject missing, failed, expired or reused tokens.
- Keep the secret key on the server only.
- Rate-limit each form by IP and by email or account.
- New accounts must verify their email before they can [send invites / use AI / start a trial].
- Log rejected attempts with the reason (no personal data) so I can see the volume.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Submitting the form with curl and no token is rejected.
2. Reusing a token that already passed is rejected.
3. Filling the honeypot field is rejected.
4. A real user in a normal browser signs up with no extra steps beyond the widget.
5. The siteverify secret never appears in the page source.
acceptance_checks: Submitting the form with curl and no token is rejected.
Reusing a token that already passed is rejected.
Filling the honeypot field is rejected.
A real user in a normal browser signs up with no extra steps beyond the widget.
The siteverify secret never appears in the page source.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Fake accounts, a spam-filled inbox, email sending suspended for bounces, card-testing fees and disputes, and AI bills run up by scripts.

entries.name: Feature flag
needs: ship code but keep the feature off
turn off the new thing without rolling back
let only me test it in production
roll a feature out to some users first
entries.summary: A named on and off switch the code checks at runtime. You deploy with the feature off, turn it on for everyone, some users or just yourself, and turn it off fast if it breaks.
need_when: Risky changes, payment changes, anything you want to undo without a rollback.
You want to try something in production before users see it.
skip_when: Small fixes. Every flag is a branch in your code that you have to remove later.

ways.title: Environment variable flags
ways.how: Read FEATURE_X_ENABLED at startup.
ways.tradeoff: Dead simple. Changing a flag needs a restart or redeploy, and it is all or nothing.

ways.title: A flags table with an admin switch
ways.how: django-waffle, Flipper for Rails, or your own table with a cached lookup.
ways.tradeoff: Flip without deploying and target staff or a list of users. More code, and the lookup needs caching.

ways.title: A flag service
ways.how: Unleash and GrowthBook are open source and self-hostable. PostHog also has feature flags.
ways.tradeoff: Percent rollouts and targeting built in. Another service and SDK in your stack.

entries.prompt:
Put [feature] behind a feature flag named [flag_name].

Requirements:
- Default off in every environment.
- One helper, is_enabled(flag, user), used everywhere. No scattered environment reads.
- Support three states: off, on for everyone, on for a list of staff user ids.
- When off: the feature's routes return 404, its UI is hidden and its scheduled jobs skip.
- Log flag changes with who and when.
- Add a dated TODO to remove the flag once it has been fully on for a while.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. With the flag off, the feature can't be reached by URL.
2. Turning it on for one staff user shows it only to them.
3. Turning it off hides it again without a code change.
4. Tests cover both the on and off states.
5. Scheduled jobs for the feature do nothing while it's off.
acceptance_checks: With the flag off, the feature can't be reached by URL.
Turning it on for one staff user shows it only to them.
Turning it off hides it again without a code change.
Tests cover both the on and off states.
Scheduled jobs for the feature do nothing while it's off.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Every risky change becomes a full rollback, and half-built features leak to users.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal uses environment flags (for example CJ_BILLING_MEASUREMENTS_ENABLED) set per service in a small Compose override file that each release must include. Its release guard compares environment keys between the live and new stack and aborts on any flag change that isn't named in an explicit allow rule for one service, one key and one exact change.

entries.name: Health checks and safe deploys
needs: the site goes down every time I deploy
know my app is broken before users tell me
the new version started before the database was ready
roll back automatically if the deploy is bad
entries.summary: Small URLs your platform calls to ask two things: is the process alive (liveness), and can it serve traffic right now, with the database, cache and migrations in order (readiness). Deploy tools wait for readiness before sending traffic to a new version and keep the old one if it never gets there.
need_when: Anything with users, and any automated deploy.
skip_when: Rarely. Even a hobby app benefits from a readiness check and an outside uptime ping.

ways.title: Two endpoints in your app
ways.how: /health/ (process up, no dependency calls) and /health/ready/ (database, cache, schema). Point Docker HEALTHCHECK, Coolify health checks or Kubernetes probes at the readiness one.
ways.tradeoff: A readiness check that tests too much can flap and take the site down on a minor issue.

ways.title: Health-gated rolling or blue-green deploys
ways.how: Start the new container, wait for readiness, switch the proxy, then stop the old one.
ways.tradeoff: Needs database migrations that work with both the old and new code at once: add columns first, remove them in a later release.

ways.title: Outside monitoring
ways.how: An uptime checker for the site, and Healthchecks.io (open source) for alerts when a scheduled job stops checking in.
ways.tradeoff: Tells you something broke. It doesn't stop a bad deploy.

entries.prompt:
Add health checks and a health-gated deploy for this app.

Requirements:
- GET /health/ returns 200 when the process is running. No database calls.
- GET /health/ready/ checks the database (SELECT 1), the cache (set and read a short-lived key) and pending migrations. It returns 200 with per-dependency status JSON, or 503 if any fail. No secrets, versions or hostnames in the response.
- The container health check points at /health/ready/.
- Deploy: start the new version, wait until /health/ready/ returns 200 (timeout [90 seconds]), then switch traffic. If it never gets ready, keep the old version serving.
- Migrations in this release must work with the currently running code.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Stopping the database makes /health/ready/ return 503 within a few seconds while /health/ stays 200.
2. Deploying a build that crashes on start leaves the old version serving.
3. During a normal deploy, a curl loop every half second sees no 5xx responses (if zero downtime is the goal).
4. The health response contains no secrets or internal hostnames.
5. Health check traffic is excluded from analytics and rate limits.
acceptance_checks: Stopping the database makes /health/ready/ return 503 within a few seconds while /health/ stays 200.
Deploying a build that crashes on start leaves the old version serving.
During a normal deploy, a curl loop every half second sees no 5xx responses (if zero downtime is the goal).
The health response contains no secrets or internal hostnames.
Health check traffic is excluded from analytics and rate limits.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Every deploy causes a few minutes of errors, and a bad build stays live until someone notices.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal exposes /health/ready/, which reports database, cache and schema status. Its releases are not zero-downtime: the runbook uses a short maintenance window, says not to use the Coolify Deploy button (that redeploy replaces the whole stack, including Postgres and Redis), and doesn't end maintenance until all six services are healthy and /health/ready/ returns 200. If any health gate fails, the release guard runs the captured rollback automatically.

entries.name: Caching and invalidation
needs: the same slow query runs on every page load
users see old data after they save
cache the AI answer so I don't pay for it twice
one user saw another user's page
entries.summary: Keeping the result of slow or costly work for a while so the next request can reuse it. The hard parts are the key (it must include everything the result depends on, including the user) and knowing when the saved copy is out of date.
need_when: The same expensive query, API call or AI call runs again and again with the same inputs.
skip_when: The page is already fast. Fix slow queries with indexes before adding a cache.

ways.title: Content-addressed keys with a TTL
ways.how: Build the key from a hash of every input (model name, prompt, settings, user id where relevant) and set an expiry. New inputs make a new key, so nothing needs deleting.
ways.tradeoff: No invalidation bugs. Only works when the result depends only on the inputs in the key.

ways.title: Redis or Valkey with delete on write
ways.how: Cache reads in Redis or Valkey and delete the key in the same code path that saves the data.
ways.tradeoff: Fresh data after saves. Every write path must remember to delete, and you need a plan for when the cache is down.

ways.title: HTTP caching
ways.how: Cache-Control and ETag headers so browsers and CDNs reuse public responses.
ways.tradeoff: Cheapest of all. Only safe for responses that are the same for everyone, or marked private.

entries.prompt:
Add caching for [slow operation] in this app.

Requirements:
- First measure: log how long the operation takes and how often it runs with the same inputs. Show me the numbers.
- Cache in [Redis/Valkey, or the framework cache]. Build each key from a prefix, a version and a hash of every input the result depends on. Include the user or tenant id for anything user-specific.
- Set a TTL of [X]. For data users edit, delete the key in the same code path that saves it.
- If the cache is unreachable, fall back to doing the work (fail open) and log a warning without the key or values. Security features such as rate limits must not fall back this way.
- Prevent a stampede: only one request rebuilds an expired key while others wait briefly or get the old value.
- Never cache responses with private data in a shared or CDN cache.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. The second identical request is at least [5x] faster, shown with timings.
2. After a user edits the data, the next read shows the new value.
3. User A never receives a cached result that belongs to user B.
4. Stopping Redis keeps the app working, just slower.
5. 100 parallel requests for an expired key run the expensive work once.
acceptance_checks: The second identical request is at least [5x] faster, shown with timings.
After a user edits the data, the next read shows the new value.
User A never receives a cached result that belongs to user B.
Stopping Redis keeps the app working, just slower.
100 parallel requests for an expired key run the expensive work once.
entries.if_you_skip_it: Stale pages after saves, users seeing each other's data, an app that dies when the cache does, and AI bills for repeat work.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal uses Redis as one cache shared by all workers when it's configured, and falls back to per-process memory otherwise. AI tone results are cached for 7 days under a SHA-256 of the model, the input and a flag, so a new input or model simply makes a new key. Its optional cache helpers fail open and log a warning without the key, because keys can contain session ids.

entries.name: CDN and static asset caching
needs: my site is slow for people in other countries
users still get the old JavaScript after I deploy
serve images and CSS faster
my server is busy sending static files
entries.summary: Serving files that are the same for everyone, like CSS, JavaScript, fonts and images, from servers close to the user, with file names that change when the content changes. Then browsers can cache them for a year, and a deploy still shows the new version at once.
need_when: Users are spread out geographically, or your app server spends time sending static files.
People report seeing an old version after a deploy.
skip_when: Your host already does this, as Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages do for built assets. Check the headers and move on.

ways.title: Hashed file names and long cache headers
ways.how: Your bundler (Vite, Next.js, webpack) or Django's ManifestStaticFilesStorage adds a content hash to each file name. Serve them with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, and keep HTML short-lived.
ways.tradeoff: The base of everything else. Free.

ways.title: WhiteNoise or your host's static serving
ways.how: For Python apps, WhiteNoise serves compressed, hashed static files with the right headers straight from the app.
ways.tradeoff: No extra service. Still served from one region unless a CDN sits in front.

ways.title: A CDN in front
ways.how: Cloudflare (free plan), Bunny or CloudFront cache static files at the edge.
ways.tradeoff: Fast everywhere. Misconfigured rules can cache private pages, so cache by path or header, not everything.

entries.prompt:
Set up static asset caching and a CDN for this app.

Requirements:
- Make every built CSS, JS, font and image file name include a content hash.
- Serve hashed files with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.
- Serve HTML with a short cache or no-cache, so a deploy shows up at once.
- Compress text assets with Brotli or gzip.
- If a CDN is added, cache only static paths (like /static/ or /assets/) and public pages. Never cache responses that set cookies or depend on the logged-in user.
- Document how to purge the CDN if a bad file ships.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. curl -I on a JS file shows the immutable cache header and a hashed name.
2. curl -I on the home page shows a short or no-cache header.
3. After a deploy, a normal reload shows the new version without a hard refresh.
4. A logged-in page is never served from the CDN cache (check the CDN's cache status header).
acceptance_checks: curl -I on a JS file shows the immutable cache header and a hashed name.
curl -I on the home page shows a short or no-cache header.
After a deploy, a normal reload shows the new version without a hard refresh.
A logged-in page is never served from the CDN cache (check the CDN's cache status header).
entries.if_you_skip_it: Slow pages far from your server, users stuck on old JavaScript that calls APIs that no longer exist, or a CDN serving one user's page to everyone.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal serves static files with WhiteNoise using CompressedManifestStaticFilesStorage, which writes compressed copies with content-hashed file names.

entries.name: Database indexes
needs: my app got slow as the data grew
this query takes seconds
the dashboard runs hundreds of queries
which columns should I index
entries.summary: Lookup structures that let the database find rows without reading the whole table. Most slow pages in young apps come from a missing index on the columns a query filters and sorts by, or from N+1 queries that run one query per row.
need_when: Pages get slower as tables grow past tens of thousands of rows.
Your query log shows the same query running once per item in a list.
skip_when: Tiny tables. Extra indexes slow down writes and take space, so add them for real queries, not just in case.

ways.title: Measure, then index what queries use
ways.how: Turn on pg_stat_statements (Postgres) or your framework's query log, find the slowest and most frequent queries, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and add an index matching the WHERE and ORDER BY columns.
ways.tradeoff: Fixes the real problems. Needs production-like data to see them.

ways.title: Composite and partial indexes
ways.how: One index on (user_id, created_at) serves 'this user's newest items'. A partial index (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) keeps it small.
ways.tradeoff: Column order matters: equality filters first, then the sort column.

ways.title: Fix N+1 queries
ways.how: Load related rows in one query: select_related and prefetch_related (Django), include (Prisma), joins or batched loaders.
ways.tradeoff: Often a bigger win than any index. Tools like django-debug-toolbar show the query count.

entries.prompt:
Find and fix slow database queries in this app.

Requirements:
- Turn on query logging or pg_stat_statements and list the 10 slowest and 10 most frequent queries.
- For each, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-like data and show whether it uses an index.
- Add indexes that match the filters and sort order, composite where needed, with equality columns first. Note that Postgres doesn't index foreign keys automatically.
- On large tables, create indexes without blocking writes (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on Postgres).
- Find N+1 query patterns in list pages and APIs and load related data in batches.
- Report the before and after timings and the query count for the main pages.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. EXPLAIN ANALYZE for the main list query shows an index scan, not a sequential scan, on a large table.
2. The main list page runs a fixed number of queries no matter how many rows it shows.
3. Before and after timings are shown for each fix.
4. Each new index is used by at least one real query.
acceptance_checks: EXPLAIN ANALYZE for the main list query shows an index scan, not a sequential scan, on a large table.
The main list page runs a fixed number of queries no matter how many rows it shows.
Before and after timings are shown for each fix.
Each new index is used by at least one real query.
entries.if_you_skip_it: An app that was fast in the demo slows to seconds per page with real data, and the database bill climbs to compensate.
entries.how_derek_runs_it: Custody Journal's journal entries have a composite index on (user, is_archived, newest date first), which matches the main entry list. Its email outbox has an index on (status, next attempt time, created time) so the sender can find due emails quickly.
